About: The Harmonic Oscillator — Why Period Ignores Amplitude

Source

Simulation
The Harmonic Oscillator — Why Period Ignores Amplitude (misconception-first, counterfactual two-well mode).
Concept
A particle in V = ½kx² oscillates as x(t) = A·cos(ωt + φ) with ω = √(k/m); the period T = 2π√(m/k) is independent of amplitude, while KE and PE trade off at constant total E = ½mv² + ½kx² = ½kA².
Serves
Reading potential-energy diagrams; SHM as the linear-restoring-force special case; energy conservation and turning points where V(x) = E.
Inquiry
Two balls released together from 0.30 m and 0.60 m — which returns first? Which slider CAN change the period? In which well do the recorder traces dephase?
Misconception target
"Larger amplitude ⇒ longer period." True in a constant-force well V = F₀|x| (T ∝ √A) — false for the spring, where F = −kx grows with the swing and amplitude cancels exactly.
Verified values
k = 20 N/m, m = 0.5 kg → ω = 6.3246 rad/s, T = 0.9935 s at BOTH A = 0.3 m and A = 0.6 m; E(A = 0.3 m) = ½kA² = 0.90 J, all potential at x = ±0.30 m.

The Harmonic Oscillator
▶ Press Play — ball releases from rest

Guided Inquiry

1 · Two balls, one spring well

Both balls sit at rest in V = ½kx² (k = 20 N/m, m = 0.50 kg). Ball 1 waits at A₁ = 0.30 m; ball 2 waits twice as far at A₂ = 0.60 m. Same well, same mass — only the release points differ.

2 · Predict — the two-ball race

Released together from rest, each swings in, out the other side, and back. Which ball completes one full cycle first?

3 · Compare the two traces

Both balls are running. Compare the two x(t) traces: how do their heights differ, and how do their zero crossings compare? Then move A₁ and A₂ to any other pair of values and compare again.

4 · Predict — what moves T?

You just saw A₁ ≠ A₂ leave T unchanged. In this spring well, which change does move the period?

5 · Why the farther ball is not slower

The arrow on each ball is the restoring force F = −kx, drawn to scale. Ball 2 is at twice ball 1’s displacement at every instant. Compare the two arrows, and compare how far each ball still has to travel.

6 · Amplitude sets energy, not the clock

Because F = −kx, doubling the amplitude doubles both the distance to cover and the force available to cover it, so A cancels out of T = 2π√(m/k). Amplitude still fixes E = ½kA² and the turning points x = ±A. A period that ignores amplitude is the fingerprint of simple harmonic motion.

01

At a glance

Two balls sit on the x-axis under an energy parabola, one released from rest at 0.30 m and the other at 0.60 m. A spring pulls both back toward x = 0, and the sim draws their positions, forces, energies and periods side by side.

What you'll learn

  • How the spring force F = −kx drives a ball released from rest.
  • How the energy ½kA² is shared between motion and the stretched spring.
  • Which settings decide the time of one full swing.
The energy well, with ball 1 and ball 2 waiting at their release points.

Moving k, m or an amplitude restarts both balls from rest. There is no friction, so a swing never dies away. With two balls showing, the KE and PE bars add the two balls together.

03

A spring pulls back in proportion to the stretch

A spring pulls a ball toward its resting place x = 0, and the pull grows as the ball moves farther out. With the direction included, this restoring force is

F = −kx
The minus sign means the force points opposite to the displacement.

A larger k is a stiffer spring and a larger pull at the same x. The energy stored in the stretched spring is V = ½kx², which is the parabola in the sim.

A ball released from rest at x = A is momentarily still there, so A is the farthest it ever goes. The swing runs from x = A out to x = −A and back, and A is called the amplitude.

See itWatch the force arrows on the two balls. Watch for: each arrow pointing back toward x = 0, and shrinking away as that ball crosses the centre.
04

Energy swaps between motion and spring, and the total stays fixed

The ledger lists kinetic energy KE = ½mv², potential energy PE = ½kx² and their sum E. With no friction, whatever PE the ball loses it gains as KE, so E stays equal to its starting value:

E = ½mv² + ½kx² = ½kA²

At the turning points x = ±A the ball is still, so all of E is PE. At x = 0 all of E is KE. For A = 0.30 m and k = 20 N/m, E = 0.90 J, so with m = 0.50 kg the ball passes the centre at 1.90 m/s.

KE and PE are equal where |x| = A/√2, which is 0.212 m for this ball. The amplitude fixes the energy: A = 0.60 m stores E = 3.60 J, four times as much.

See itOpen the ledger with one ball swinging. Watch for: the E column staying at 0.90 J while KE and PE trade places.
05

The period has no amplitude in it

Newton's second law with F = −kx gives a = −(k/m)x. The motion x(t) = A cos ωt solves this when ω² = k/m. The amplitude A only scales the cosine, so it never enters ω. One full swing takes

T = 2π/ω = 2π√(m/k)
For k = 20 N/m and m = 0.50 kg: ω = 6.3246 rad/s and T = 0.9935 s.

There is no A in this formula. A ball released from 0.30 m and one released from 0.60 m both take 0.993 s, so the race ends in a dead heat on every cycle. A period that ignores the amplitude is the mark of simple harmonic motion.

See itRun both balls with the default sliders. Watch for: T₁ = 0.993 s and T₂ = 0.993 s (= T₁), and both traces crossing zero together.
06

A farther ball has more to cover and a stronger pull

With A₂ = 2A₁, ball 2 is always at twice ball 1's displacement, so F = −kx makes its force twice as large at every instant. The same mass then gives twice the acceleration. At release, ball 1 feels 6 N and accelerates at 12 m/s², while ball 2 feels 12 N and accelerates at 24 m/s².

From rest, twice the acceleration covers twice the distance in the same time, so the extra pull exactly pays for the extra path. This balance holds only because the force grows in proportion to x.

Imagine a well where the pull is capped at a constant F₀ instead. Then T = 4√(2Am/F₀) grows with the amplitude, and a release from twice as far takes √2 times as long.

See itCompare A₁ = 0.20 m with A₂ = 0.60 m. Watch for: ball 2's arrow three times as long as ball 1's, yet both balls cross x = 0 together.
07

Only k and m change the period

In T = 2π√(m/k), a stiffer spring shortens T and a heavier ball lengthens it. The amplitude and the total energy only set how far and how fast the ball goes, not the clock.

Doubling k divides T by √2, so k = 40 N/m gives T = 0.702 s in place of 0.993 s. Quadrupling the mass doubles T, so m = 2.0 kg at k = 20 N/m gives T = 1.987 s.

Both balls follow the same change, because they share k and m. Only the amplitudes differ, and they never appear in T.

See itStiffen the spring to 40 N/m. Watch for: T₁ = T₂ = 0.702 s, shorter than before, with the traces crossing zero more often.
See itRaise the mass to 2.0 kg at k = 20 N/m. Watch for: T₁ = T₂ = 1.987 s, twice the opening value, and slower traces.
08

Where it matters

  • Tuning forks. The pitch stays the same as the sound fades, because the frequency does not depend on how large the vibration is.
  • Quartz watches. A tiny crystal vibrates at a nearly fixed frequency, and that steadiness is what keeps the watch on time.
  • Vertical spring. Hanging a ball on a spring only moves the resting place. The swing about it is still T = 2π√(m/k).
  • Small pendulum swings. The restoring force is nearly proportional to the displacement, so T = 2π√(L/g) holds for small angles only.
  • Atoms in a solid. For small displacements, each atom's bonds act like tiny springs with their own k and m.
09

Summary

In one line. A restoring force proportional to the displacement makes a smooth back-and-forth swing, and every feature of that swing follows from the one rule.

Key points

  • F = −kx, V = ½kx², and E = ½kA² stays constant during the swing.
  • T = 2π√(m/k) contains m and k only, so the amplitude does not change it.
  • A larger amplitude brings more energy, a longer path and a stronger pull, and these balance in time.

Common mix-ups

  • "A farther ball takes longer." Ball 2 covers twice the path but feels twice the pull, so both return together.
  • "More energy means a slower cycle." E = ½kA² grows with A, yet T = 2π√(m/k) does not.
  • "Every back-and-forth motion has this property." It needs a force proportional to x. A capped force gives T that grows with √A.

Things to try on your own

  • Set A₁ = A₂ and check that the two traces lie exactly on top of each other.
  • Predict T for k = 10 N/m and m = 0.50 kg, then check it in the Periods box.
  • Read the ledger at x = ±A and at x = 0, and say where E sits in each case.
